articles.title: 12 subscriptions that are no longer worth paying for in 2026
articles.summary: Between higher prices, ads and overlapping features, many popular subscriptions aren't worth the monthly drain on your bank account anymore.
articles.body:
If you buy something through a link in this article, we may earn commission.

Not that long ago, subscriptions felt simple. You paid for Netflix instead of cable, Spotify instead of buying CDs and Amazon Prime for the free shipping. But somewhere along the way, nearly every company decided your credit card deserved a recurring monthly charge. Now we're subscribing to food delivery apps, AI tools, cloud storage, fitness trackers, printer ink and enough streaming services to recreate a 2009 Comcast bill five times over.

If you really want to see how wild it's gotten, open the subscriptions tied to your Apple ID or scroll through your credit card statement for a few minutes. (Be honest, when was the last time you actually did that?) There's a decent chance you'll find at least one monthly charge you forgot existed entirely.

To be clear, this isn't about canceling everything and living like it's 1997. Some subscriptions are useful and worth every penny. But these are the ones that, for a lot of people, aren't pulling their weight anymore.

Remember when cutting the cord was supposed to save you money? We went from paying one expensive cable bill to juggling Netflix, Hulu, HBO Max, Disney+, Peacock, Paramount+ and three others you forgot were still auto-renewing. Worse, a lot of them now charge more while also showing ads — nothing like the privilege of paying to watch commercials.

The smarter move is to rotate services rather than subscribe to all of them year-round. Subscribe for a month, binge what you want, cancel it, then move on to the next one. Unless you're constantly using a specific platform every week, you're paying $20 a month just to scroll past the same five shows every night before rewatching The Office again.

Still dealing with a menagerie of remotes every time you want to watch TV? Stop the insanity with this easy and intuitive top-seller (which happens to be the newest model) that can replace 'em all. You'll be able to effortlessly switch between the news, sports, live TV and your favorite streaming platforms for easy access to millions of shows and movies. If you have a 4K TV, the Fire TV Stick 4K Max is the most powerful streaming stick Amazon makes.

Food delivery apps felt like a lifesaver a few years ago. Busy night? Tap a button and tacos magically appear at your front door. But in the past few years, the math got weird. Thanks to delivery fees, service charges, tips and inflated menu prices, your $14 burrito bowl becomes a $31 hit to your bank account.

At the risk of sounding like a personal finance guy with a YouTube channel and a microphone headset, most of us probably don't need to be ordering takeout as often as we do — especially not paying extra to have someone bring us a lukewarm burrito bowl from three miles away. A little planning and a trip to Aldi or Trader Joe's can easily cover a week of quick meals, many of which are super easy to make: just pop them in the microwave, oven or air fryer, and you're done.

If you're addicted to the food delivery apps, consider this your recovery tool. Frozen meals, chicken nuggets, salmon, roasted vegetables — this thing makes all of them faster than most delivery drivers can get to your house, and without the service fees, tips or mysterious $11 delivery surcharge attached to your burrito bowl.

Dealusy Glass Food Storage Containers, 10-Piece Set

This is the one on the list I thought most about not including because dedicated password managers are excellent products. But Safari and Chrome have gotten insanely good at password management, which means a lot of people are paying monthly for password managers even though they already rely mostly on the built-in tools on their phones and computers.

If you want to take your online security seriously, a hardware security key adds an extra layer of protection to important accounts like email, banking and cloud storage. It's like a house key for your digital life. Even if someone figures out your password, they still can't get inside without the physical key itself.

Audiobook subscriptions are dangerous because, like fitness apps, they are somewhat aspirational. You set a goal for yourself at the beginning of the year to become the person who listens to 45 books a year while jogging at sunrise and organizing your home. By June, you're still halfway through chapter three of the same history book you started in February.

For heavy listeners, Audible and similar services can absolutely be worth the money. But before committing, it's worth checking what you already have access to. Spotify includes audiobooks on paid plans, and most public libraries offer free access to large catalogs through apps like Libby or Hoopla — no subscription required. A lot of people are paying monthly to slowly build a digital bookshelf of books they fully intend to listen to "eventually," without realizing a free option was sitting right there.

If your goal really is to consume more books, investing in a dedicated reading device may make more sense than endlessly paying for audiobook subscriptions you barely use. Bonus: You can use your Bluetooth headphones to listen to your audiobooks from this Kindle Paperwhite as well.

Printer ink subscriptions might be one of the clearest examples of how absolutely everything became a subscription. Most people barely print anymore aside from shipping labels, school forms and the occasional tax document.

If you're still printing constantly for work or running a home office, an ink subscription may make sense. But for casual users, a cheap monochrome laser printer is usually the better long-term move. The toner lasts forever, the printers are surprisingly reliable and — perhaps most importantly — they don't email you every time you print a document. And if you'd rather not commit to a subscription at all, buying ink only when you need it is almost always cheaper for anyone printing sporadically.

Yes, this printer comes with a "free trial" and tons of bloatware, but here's the thing: You don't have to install it or subscribe to anything for it to work well and reliably.

Canon Pixma TS4320 Wireless Color Inkjet Printer

A lot of people now have what can only be described as a subscription smoothie of fitness apps. Strava, MyFitnessPal, Apple Fitness+, Peloton, meditation apps, macro trackers, sleep apps — at a certain point, you're paying monthly to generate colorful graphs showing how tired you are.

Modern smartwatches and phones already do a pretty impressive job handling most of this stuff for free. If you're training for a marathon or following a specific daily program, absolutely keep the app you love. Right now, I pay for Strava and use it almost daily, but if you haven't opened it since January and it's still charging your credit card every month, it might be time for the digital equivalent of cleaning out your garage.

Many of these apps offer free trials or pared-down, no-cost experiences that let you check them out for a while before committing. For the ones that you do use, keep an eye out for lifetime subscriptions. I snagged a lifetime subscription for Lose It! a few years back, and it has saved me quite a bit in fees since then.

This smartwatch boasts upgrades like 24-hour battery life, updated sleep score features, integrated exercise modes and heart-rate monitoring, all without a subscription.

2025 and 2026 became the years of paying monthly for ChatGPT, Claude, Midjourney and three other apps that promised to "revolutionize productivity" before mostly just helping write slightly more professional-sounding emails.

To be clear, AI tools can absolutely be worth paying for — especially if you use them every day. The problem is that a lot of people now have overlapping subscriptions that basically do the same thing. In most cases, one good AI subscription is plenty. You probably don't need an entire Avengers team's worth of chatbots helping you make your weekly grocery lists.

Many modern laptops and tablets have AI tools built directly into the operating system — like Apple Intelligence in the MacBook Air — that include everything from writing assistance and image cleanup to summarizing notifications and organizing files. Upgrading the device you already use every day may have a bigger impact on productivity than subscribing to multiple AI services.

Just note that Apple recently raised prices on MacBooks and some iPads due to increased memory costs and widespread shortages. You'll want to keep an eye out for good deals on these devices during events like Amazon Prime Day or Black Friday so you can save a little cash while you upgrade.

Cloud storage subscriptions usually start innocently enough. You run out of space once, upgrade to the next tier and suddenly you're paying monthly to store 14,000 screenshots, blurry dog photos and a video from a concert you haven't watched since 2022.

A surprising number of people upgrade storage plans instead of just deleting junk. Modern phones are packed with duplicate photos, giant video files and random downloads, all of which are driving up your monthly bill.

I'm an Apple user, but this drive should work with any phone that has a USB-C connection. Plug this drive into your iPhone with the USB-C cable. Open Photos, pick what you want, hit Share, then tap Save to Files. Choose the SSD and a folder, and you're done. Now you can go back and delete the copied photos and free up space on your device. The drive's already formatted correctly, so it just works — just make sure your phone's got enough juice since SSDs pull a little more power than other devices.

Retail memberships are starting to feel a lot like streaming services. Amazon Prime, Walmart+, Instacart+, Target Circle 360 — companies realized people will happily pay monthly fees in exchange for faster shipping, grocery delivery and the occasional "exclusive deal" on paper towels.

The issue with these is similar to that of streaming services: most overlap heavily. They're also designed to remove every barrier between you and a purchase — fast delivery, free shipping, one-click checkout — which is great when you really need something, but quite expensive when you don't. That small friction of a shipping cost or a two-day wait used to make you pause and reconsider. At most, I would pick the one membership that fits how you shop and leave the rest behind.

Retail memberships encourage convenience spending and impulse buying. Organizing your pantry, freezer and storage space makes it easier to buy intentionally in bulk and use what you already have.

If you bought a family computer in the early 2000s (Gateway, anyone?), there was about a 97% chance someone at the store also convinced you to buy antivirus software. Back then, that wasn't necessarily bad advice. The internet was still the Wild West, and clicking the wrong pop-up ad could mean destroying your entire family's desktop computer in seconds.

Modern computers are much better at protecting themselves now. Antivirus subscriptions can still make sense for older relatives, shared family computers or people who download sketchy files from the internet. Still, many casual users are paying annual fees for protection they no longer need.

Instead of paying yearly for bloated antivirus software, investing in a modern mesh router like this Amazon Eero 6+ may do more to improve both your Wi-Fi and your home network security. Modern routers receive regular security updates and help protect the growing number of connected devices in your home, from laptops and phones to smart TVs, video doorbells and gaming consoles.

Adobe Creative Suite or other photo editing apps

Adobe subscriptions make perfect sense for professional photographers, designers and video editors. If your paycheck depends on Photoshop or Lightroom, this isn't about you. But many users are still paying professional-level subscription prices just to occasionally crop vacation photos and increase the brightness by 12%.

Phones and free editing apps have gotten incredibly good. For most people, the built-in editing tools on an iPhone or Android device already handle 90% of what they actually need. Paying monthly for a massive suite of creative software to edit two Christmas card photos a year is a complete waste of money. Additionally, if all you're doing is editing photos, just get Lightroom; there's no need to spend money on a bundle of video editing and design apps.

For many people, Adobe's Lightroom-only plan makes a lot more sense than paying for the entire Creative Cloud package, which has a monthly cost of around $90. At $84 for a year (that's $7/month), Lightroom still gives you seriously powerful editing tools without making you pay for dozens of professional apps you'll likely never open.

Outdoor apps have gotten really great. Offline maps, trail conditions, GPS tracking, campsite info — they're incredibly useful tools, especially for hiking, backpacking and trail running. The problem is that a lot of outdoorsy people (like me) have five overlapping subscriptions.

Apps like AllTrails+, Gaia GPS and onX Backcountry absolutely have their place, especially for serious hikers and backcountry users. But many casual hikers don't need multiple premium subscriptions just to find a local trail with decent parking and a cool lake at the end. In a lot of cases, one app is more than enough.

Instead of paying monthly for multiple overlapping hiking and navigation apps, a GPS watch with built-in mapping and offline navigation may make more sense for people who spend a lot of time outdoors.

articles.title: Fluence Has a $6.4 Billion Backlog but Pushed $400 Million of Deliveries Out. Is the AI-Power Story Breaking?
articles.summary: In its August 5 results, Fluence Energy ended the fiscal third quarter with a $6.4 billion backlog, yet about $400 million of project deliveries moved into f...
articles.body:
In its August 5 results, Fluence Energy ended the fiscal third quarter with a $6.4 billion backlog, yet about $400 million of project deliveries moved into fiscal 2027. The tension between demand and execution sits at the heart of the stock. Fluence Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: FLNC ) has become an AI-power proxy because batteries can help data centers secure capacity and stabilize grids. Its latest numbers show how a large revenue opportunity can still produce disappointing shareholder economics.

Battery energy storage solutions. Photo from Fluence Energy website

There is substance behind the optimistic view. Fiscal third-quarter revenue increased 7.9% to $649.8 million, order intake exceeded $1.44 billion, and backlog reached $6.4 billion. Fluence said its data-center business totaled about $850 million, including $550 million of awards tied to a hyperscaler. That pipeline places battery storage inside identifiable AI infrastructure projects rather than leaving it as a broad grid theme.

Execution is the problem. Gross margin fell to 5.1% from 14.8% a year earlier, and net loss widened to $44.3 million. Management said about $400 million of project deliveries shifted into fiscal 2027. It reduced the midpoint of full-year revenue guidance from $3.4 billion to $3.0 billion and moved the adjusted EBITDA midpoint from positive $50 million to negative $10 million. A large backlog offers limited comfort if timing slips and project economics deteriorate.

Professional investors became more numerous before the quarterly report. Insider Monkey counted 39 hedge funds holding Fluence Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ:FLNC) at the end of Q2, up from 31 in Q1. Point72 Asset Management reported 1,301,799 shares as of June 30, while D. E. Shaw reported 3,194,735. Those positions offer a snapshot of long exposure; they do not identify either manager's present view or complete portfolio.

Reported short interest was substantial. The August 14 settlement showed 25.45 million shares short, up 13.9% from 22.35 million on July 31, with 2.7 days to cover. Published float estimates diverge sharply, making the raw position and its change more dependable than a percentage. The positioning creates squeeze potential while raising the burden of proof.

The AI-power story remains under pressure because Fluence has yet to convert demand into reliable margins and delivery timing. Management now needs to show that delayed projects remain profitable and the data-center business turns into cash. Investors should track gross margin by project mix, working-capital use, and the portion of backlog that converts each quarter. Those measures will separate a temporary schedule problem from contracts that were priced too aggressively.

articles.title: RingCentral Says Paid-AI Customers Now Represent 13% of ARR as Revenue Grew 6%. Has the Market Already Priced It In?
articles.summary: On July 23, RingCentral said customers using at least one paid native AI product represented about 13% of annual recurring revenue, and that measure had doub...
articles.body:
On July 23, RingCentral said customers using at least one paid native AI product represented about 13% of annual recurring revenue, and that measure had doubled year over year. That gives its AI strategy a measurable commercial foothold. By September 2, RingCentral, Inc. (NYSE: RNG ) had already gained about 141% over the preceding year and traded near a four-year high, leaving investors to decide whether a revived business can keep compounding.

Second-quarter results give the bulls evidence. Revenue rose 5.9% to $657 million, subscription revenue increased 5.8% to $634 million, and GAAP operating margin reached 7.7%. Customers using paid native AI products represented 13% of annual recurring revenue, double the year-earlier level. That measure describes the ARR attached to customers using a paid AI product; it is neither standalone AI revenue nor proof that AI caused every dollar in the cohort. The distinction matters when investors price AI-driven expansion. Management also raised its full-year revenue range, lifted free-cash-flow guidance to $615 million to $625 million, and increased the dividend 67%.

The challenge is that headline growth remains modest. AI adoption can deepen customer spending, but communications software is competitive and switching costs are not absolute. Microsoft, Zoom, contact-center specialists, and newer AI-native services can pressure pricing. The stock's large rebound also means improving profitability is no longer a secret, and the margin of safety has narrowed with the rerating.

Hedge funds became slightly more numerous during Q2. Insider Monkey counted 27 funds holding RingCentral, Inc. (NYSE:RNG), up from 25 in Q1. AQR Capital Management reported 1,537,795 shares as of June 30. That snapshot records historical positioning rather than proving how the fund views the stock today.

Short interest was meaningful but declining. The August 14 settlement showed 7.06 million shares short, or 9.12% of float, down 7.7% from 7.65 million on July 31, with 3.8 days to cover. The decline does not reveal why individual traders changed exposure.

RingCentral's AI story is becoming measurable because the ARR share tied to customers using at least one paid product, rather than demo activity, has doubled. The remaining question is whether AI can lift total company growth beyond the mid-single digits while margins expand. Net retention, the ARR share tied to customers using paid AI products, seat growth, and free cash flow should move together if the strategy is working. A higher AI-usage percentage alone could otherwise reflect adoption inside a business whose overall revenue pool is expanding too slowly to reward long-term shareholders adequately in today's market.

articles.title: WhiteFiber’s Cloud and Colocation Revenue Grew With 6 Million Shares Sold Short. Is This AI Data-Center Bet a Squeeze or a Trap?
articles.summary: WhiteFiber’s August 12 filing showed that second-quarter colocation and cloud-services revenue both increased, while 6.04 million shares were sold short at t...
articles.body:
WhiteFiber's August 12 filing showed that second-quarter colocation and cloud-services revenue both increased, while 6.04 million shares were sold short at the August 14 settlement. That pairing captures the market's argument over an ambitious AI-infrastructure buildout. WhiteFiber, Inc. (NASDAQ: WYFI ) describes itself as a vertically integrated provider of AI-optimized data centers and GPU cloud services. The model offers exposure to both the buildings and the computing capacity inside them, but it also requires unusually heavy capital and precise execution.

The attraction is easy to see. Dense AI clusters need power, cooling, networking, and specialized operations. WhiteFiber can earn colocation revenue while also selling compute through its cloud platform. Second-quarter colocation revenue rose to $4.7 million from $1.7 million, while cloud-services revenue climbed to $23.8 million from $16.6 million, although the quarter included a $12.3 million customer-termination fee that substantially offset lost recurring GPU-service revenue from that customer. If capacity fills and customers sign longer contracts, fixed infrastructure can produce meaningful operating leverage.

The capital structure keeps the story speculative. At June 30, WhiteFiber had $56.1 million of cash, $83.2 million of debt, $222.6 million carrying value of convertible notes, and a $28.6 million working-capital deficit. On August 21, it closed $310 million of new 5% convertible notes due 2032 and received about $298.5 million net. It used $118.5 million of the proceeds plus 6.3 million shares to exchange $198.15 million principal of its older notes. The refinancing improved liquidity, but it also added interest expense and potential dilution.

Professional investors were moving in opposite directions. Insider Monkey's database showed 16 hedge funds holding WhiteFiber, Inc. (NASDAQ:WYFI) at the end of Q2, down from 17 in Q1. Citadel Advisors reported 1,174,300 shares as of June 30.

Short positioning is a defining technical feature. The August 14 settlement showed 6.04 million shares short, down 6.5% from 6.47 million on July 31, with 4.1 days to cover. Good contract or utilization news could force covering; disappointing execution would strengthen the fundamental bear case.

WhiteFiber is both a squeeze candidate and a fundamental test. Scarce AI-ready infrastructure creates upside, while leverage and losses give bearish investors a case. Investors should focus on contracted power, utilization, recurring revenue, debt terms, and cash conversion. Execution now matters more than ambition. The August refinancing provides capital to build, but a commercially attractive data center can still produce poor equity returns when interest costs or dilution absorb the upside.

articles.title: Monolithic Power Revenue Jumped 48%. Can AI Power Chips Keep the Momentum Going?
articles.summary: On July 30, Monolithic Power Systems reported second-quarter revenue of $980.6 million, up 47.6% from a year earlier and 21.9% sequentially. The pace puts it...
articles.body:
On July 30, Monolithic Power Systems reported second-quarter revenue of $980.6 million, up 47.6% from a year earlier and 21.9% sequentially. The pace puts its AI opportunity into reported results. Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ: MPWR ) does not sell AI accelerators. It supplies the power-management components that help those expensive processors operate efficiently, making the company a picks-and-shovels bet on rising compute density.

Close-up of Silicon Die are being Extracted from Semiconductor Wafer and Attached to Substrate by Pick and Place Machine. Computer Chip Manufacturing at Fab. Semiconductor Packaging Process.

That position creates a clear advantage. More powerful accelerators require increasingly sophisticated voltage regulation and power delivery, creating opportunities for higher content per system. Monolithic Power's broad product portfolio and engineering relationships can make designs sticky once qualified. Q2 gross margin of 55.2% indicates that recent growth preserved the basic economics of the business. Investors should still separate data-center momentum from companywide demand, because a strong AI category can coexist with softer orders across automotive, industrial, storage, and consumer applications. That distinction matters most if ordering momentum begins to slow.

The risks sit in expectations and concentration. Semiconductor demand is cyclical, customers can redesign systems, and large buyers have leverage over pricing. AI infrastructure orders may be strong while consumer, automotive, or industrial markets weaken. After a powerful rerating, the stock needs more than rapid revenue growth to justify elevated expectations. It needs confidence that those gains can persist without inventory corrections or competitive losses.

Hedge-fund ownership expanded sharply during Q2. Insider Monkey tracked 69 funds holding Monolithic Power Systems, Inc. (NASDAQ:MPWR) at quarter-end, up from 49 in Q1. Adage Capital Management reported 96,352 shares as of June 30. Citadel also disclosed puts covering 85,300 shares, a reminder that 13F long and option positions can serve different purposes within a broader strategy.

Short interest is comparatively moderate. The August 14 settlement showed 1.84 million shares short, or 3.88% of float, down 13.4% from July 31, with 2.7 days to cover. Forced covering is unlikely to be the main engine of the investment case. Pricing alone cannot protect a richly valued cyclical supplier from weaker demand.

Monolithic Power is turning AI power complexity into reported revenue. Q2 supports that thesis, while the valuation leaves little room for an ordinary semiconductor pause. Investors should watch design wins, customer diversity, and gross margin. Another quarter of strong enterprise-data revenue, without margin deterioration or an offsetting correction elsewhere, would provide the cleanest confirmation. That combination would show the company is gaining valuable content rather than benefiting from a temporary surge in customer ordering.

articles.title: Nvidia Says Memory Pricing Has Turned ‘Extreme’ and Is ‘Headed Even Higher Into Next Year,’ But Its Own Price Increases Are Already Executed
articles.summary: CFO Colette Kress noted "extreme pricing conditions in memory" on the Q2 earnings call.
articles.body:
Nvidia (NVDA) CFO Colette Kress told investors last week that the company is seeing "extreme pricing conditions in memory," that the increases have "exceeded our prior expectations," and that they are "headed even higher into next year." Colette Kress said this in prepared remarks on Nvidia's fiscal second-quarter earnings call on Aug. 26, and then delivered the line companies almost never say plainly: "As a result, we are resetting expectations today."

Memory is not an exotic part. It is the DRAM in a phone, the RAM in a laptop, the storage in a game console, and one of the most expensive ingredients in a graphics card… and three companies make nearly all of it. Kress was describing the market for AI server memory, not the shelf price of a laptop, and Nvidia said nothing at all about consumer devices. But those products draw on the same suppliers and the same fabs, which is why a chip company's margin guidance is worth reading even if you never buy a chip.

The guidance is where the admission gets specific. Gross margin was 75% in the quarter that was just reported. Kress guided to 74% in the current quarter and told analysts that Nvidia expects "margins to bottom in Q4 in the 71% to 72% range before settling at 72% to 73% in [fiscal 2028] as executed price increases take effect in Q1." Executed, not contemplated. Nvidia is absorbing part of the memory bill and passing part of it forward, and it has already decided how much.

Sponsored Content: Invest in the Platform Giving Everyday Investors Access to Private Markets

The company also volunteered the cause, which is the unusual part. "Memory scarcity today is being driven in large part by the AI buildout itself," Kress said, and "unlike a component that simply raises our cost with no offset benefit, tighter memory supply is a symptom of the same demand surge that's driving our own growth." Nvidia is not presenting itself as a bystander to the shortage.

It is also the largest single buyer inside it. Nvidia's supplier purchase commitments stood at roughly $279 billion in its most recent quarterly filing — capacity reserved years ahead of when the parts are needed. Tom's Hardware reports that about $160 billion of that relates to memory specifically. That split is not obviously a disclosed line item in the filing, and it should be read as that outlet's reporting rather than as a company figure.

articles.title: TCS HyperVault to invest Rs 70,000 crore in AI data centre in Hyderabad
articles.summary: TCS HyperVault to invest ₹70,000 crore in a 1GW AI data centre campus on 264 acres in Hyderabad, creating 7,000 jobs and supporting AI workloads.
articles.body: HYDERABAD: One of India’s largest artificial intelligence data centre campuses is all set to come up in Hyderabad with TCS HyperVault, a subsidiary of Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), announcing plans to invest Rs 70,000 crore for a gigawatt-scale facility in Hyderabad.It will cater to frontier AI companies like OpenAI, hyperscalers and global enterprises.TCS has been allocated 264 acres for the project at Bharat Future City that is expected to create about 7,000 direct and indirect jobs across technical, construction, engineering and operations roles.The project is expected to become functional within 18 to 24 months.HyperVault CEO and managing director Deepesh Kiran Nanda said the campus would be designed for high rack-density compute, liquid cooling, large power blocks and next-generation GPU systems.He said the facility would support future advances in AI hardware.“This will be the first time that India will witness high rack density compute of more than 170 kW. The data centre will be on a par or even ahead of anything that has been built globally,” he said.The campus, to be developed in phases based on customer demand and evolving technology requirements, is expected to incorporate green energy and water-neutral design principles.It is being designed for high-density GPU deployments and will support AI training, inference and advanced computing workloads, TCS said.Telangana competing with China, Germany & Japan, says CMThe investment was announced after a high-level TCS delegation led by its CEO & managing director K Krithivasan met Telangana chief minister A Revanth Reddy at the secretariat on Saturday afternoon and exchanged MoUs.The announcement comes months after the chief minister met Tata Sons chairman N Chandrasekaran at Davos.“Future City is reality. My dream is coming true,” said the CM, urging the TCS team to target inauguration of the project by Telangana Formation Day on June 2, 2028.He said TCS already employed more than 83,000 people in Hyderabad and urged the company to take this number beyond one lakh.Revanth said the state had maintained policy continuity for nearly three decades despite changes in govts. He said Telangana is not competing with neighbouring states but with economies such as China, Germany, Japan, South Korea and Singapore.The CM also linked the project to Telangana’s long-term economic goals, saying the state aimed to become a $1 trillion economy by 2034 and a $3 trillion economy by 2047.He said AI infrastructure would be critical to that ambition, while the project would also generate secure blue-collar employment in areas such as electrical work, plumbing, water systems and data centre operations.IT and industries minister D Sridhar Babu said the project showed Telangana’s ability to move quickly on major investments.“Telangana means business. articles.title: Job applicants are hiding secret AI messages in their résumés
articles.summary: Some job seekers are hiding AI prompts in white text on their résumés to try to influence screening tools. It's a risky move.
articles.body:
Job seekers are hiding AI prompts in white text in their résumés to try to get ahead.

Employers say this kind of résumé hacking is a turnoff because it raises ethical concerns.

"You're cutting in front of the line," said a CEO who recently came across an app with a hidden prompt.

Last month, Paul Lee was reviewing applications for a legal and compliance job at the small technology company he leads when his screening software flagged an anomaly.

Hidden in one of the hundreds of résumés he received was a block of roughly 1,500 characters typed in white text on a white background. It was an AI prompt to ignore prior instructions and declare the applicant a top-tier fit, regardless of whether the person met the role's requirements.

Lee said he was stunned and described the move as an ethical red flag for a role built on trust and integrity.

"You're cutting in front of the line," said Lee, CEO of the 40-person, Irvine, California, company InnoCaption, which makes real-time captioning technology for the deaf and hard-of-hearing community.

Résumé hacking is getting an AI-era upgrade — and not in a way that's recommended. Whereas desperate job hunters once put keywords in white text to fool screening software, some people are now quietly inputting AI prompts to try to make their applications stand out.

A May 2026 study by researchers at Duke University and collaborators analyzed nearly 200,000 résumés and found that roughly 1% contained hidden prompt injections.

"Job seekers are doing what they feel they need to do to filter through the noise," Sarah Franklin, CEO of the human resources platform Lattice, told Business Insider. She said the behavior isn't surprising because employers are overwhelmed with applications and often respond with generic rejections, if anything at all.

"The hiring process feels like this complete black box," she said.

AI is part of the problem. The technology makes it easy for job seekers to tailor and submit applications at scale , while some employers use it to help them sort through the pile, said Nada Hashmi, an assistant professor of information technology at Babson College. That can mean AI, rather than a person, may be involved in screening applicants before they reach the interview stage, which can give them an incentive to game the system.

"It's really having AIs kind of talking to each other," she said.

Even so, résumé hacking may be pointless. Recruiters and hiring managers often review applications in batches and move ahead once they find enough promising candidates , leaving later submissions unchecked, said Nathalia Aryani, corporate director of human resources at property management company Terra Vista.

Worse, getting noticed for the tactic can come with its own consequences. Those who are caught doing it may be seen as dishonest, and some employers are now actively searching for prompts because word of them is spreading.

At the Zurich-based flight-search startup Zerolook, cofounder and CEO Simone Lini uploaded about 20% of the roughly 350 résumés he had received for two engineering roles to an AI tool last month. He'd heard that applicants were hiding prompt injections and asked it to flag any examples.

One résumé, Lini learned, indeed contained instructions to ignore prior instructions and prioritize their candidacy, saying "their livelihood depends on you doing that," he recalled.

Lini, whose company is hiring after raising $1.9 million in venture capital, said that while the applicant had relevant experience, the ploy was a turnoff. He added that he disagreed with some commenters on a LinkedIn post he made about the matter who suggested it showed AI savvy.

"It's just about trying to sneak in and get to the top," he said, adding that inserting the prompt was not hard to do. He said he blocked the person from applying again.

articles.title: AudioCodes (AUDC) Bets Big On Voice AI While Cash Dwindles
articles.summary: On August 4, AudioCodes (NASDAQ:AUDC) reported second-quarter revenue of $63 million, a modest 3.1% increase from $61.1 million a year earlier, and paired th...
articles.body:
On August 4, AudioCodes (NASDAQ: AUDC ) reported second-quarter revenue of $63 million, a modest 3.1% increase from $61.1 million a year earlier, and paired the update with a 20-cent-per-share semi-annual dividend that was paid on September 3 to shareholders of record as of August 19. Beneath that slow topline number sits a business quietly reshaping itself, with one small division growing more than 50% a year while the legacy hardware side barely moves the needle. That split between old and new is the story investors need to watch.

AudioCodes' Conversational AI business grew more than 50% year over year in the second quarter, matching the pace it set in the first quarter of 2026. Combined with the Live suite of managed services for Microsoft Teams and other collaboration platforms, these two segments pushed annual recurring revenue up 20% year over year to $84 million as of June 30. Recurring revenue compounds quietly, and a growing slice of AudioCodes now runs on that basis rather than resetting every quarter.

Microsoft Teams-related sales climbed 5% year over year, a smaller number but one built on an already established customer base rather than a new product line. Voice AI Connect and Live Hub, the products built for contact centers, delivered what the company called record bookings during the quarter, with new customer wins and expansion inside existing accounts both cited as drivers. Meeting Insights, a newer meeting-intelligence product, is still in the traction-building stage, but its pipeline is expanding.

Services revenue, at $34.6 million, grew 6.2% year over year, twice the pace of total revenue, meaning subscriptions and managed offerings are gaining share of the business rather than one-time hardware sales.

Total revenue growth of 3.1% is the number that matters most for a company still generating the bulk of its business outside AI, and it shows the core is barely expanding. GAAP operating margin came in at 5.1%, and GAAP net income was just $0.5 million, or two cents a share, on $63 million of revenue. That is a thin cushion for a company simultaneously funding buybacks and a dividend.

On a non-GAAP basis, net income actually slipped to $3.9 million from $4.1 million a year earlier, even though per-share earnings rose slightly because AudioCodes has been steadily shrinking its share count. During the quarter, the company spent $8.9 million buying back 950,133 shares, and cash, deposits, and investments fell to $64.2 million as of June 30, from $75.7 million at the end of 2025. Operating cash flow of $6.1 million for the quarter did not come close to covering what went out the door for buybacks.

articles.title: Nvidia’s Hugging Face Deal Is a Hedge against Broadcom’s Custom Silicon Threat
articles.summary: NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) has officially committed billions on AI developer platform Hugging Face for a $12.9 billion. The deal signifies the chipmake...
articles.body:
NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) has officially committed billions on AI developer platform Hugging Face for a $12.9 billion. The deal signifies the chipmaker's move beyond hardware and up the AI stack.

The AI chipmaker buying the open-source model hub millions of developers are already using reads differently when compared to Broadcom's earlier forecast to double its AI chip revenue to roughly $230 billion in fiscal 2028.

Even though AVGO is facing increased competition in Google's TPU programs, it is also gaining ground with customers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. This makes Nvidia's recent move look more like insurance rather than opportunism.

In response to the acquisition, Needham analyst Rajvindra Gill reiterated a Buy rating on Nvidia on September 4, assigning a $300.00 price target.

"Yesterday, NVIDIA announced its agreement to buy Hugging Face for $12.930BN. Hugging Face is the open source platform for hosting open source and open weight models and datasets enabling developers to easily access ready-to-use models instead of building and training them from scratch."

Nvidia's $12.9 billion deal would give it a platform that is home to more than 18 million developers, researchers and creators. This platform hosts more than 3 million models, 500,000 datasets, and 1 million applications. Hugging Face is Nvidia's way of remaining central in the AI theme.

Reuters BreakingViews calls the deal Nvidia's strategic insurance policy that helps it protect market share against custom chips built by major tech clients. Regardless of which chip trains or serves a model, Hugging Face gives Nvidia a major touchpoint with developers higher up the AI stack. That is a layer of the ecosystem that gives the AI chipmaker a degree of independence.

The bear case, however, is that even though the chip giant has just agreed to spend billions on the "Switzerland of AI," Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has committed to hardware neutrality.

" Hugging Face will remain an open platform for the entire AI ecosystem. Developers will choose the models they want, the frameworks they want, the clouds and inference service providers they want, and the computing platforms they want. Nvidia Compute will not be required to build on or deploy through Hugging Face."

This makes Nvidia both strategically and publicly pressured to keep Hugging Face open to AMD and other rivals.

Some of Nvidia's customers already hold strong incentives to reduce their reliance on expensive GPUs that it provides, with the deal strengthening its position but not completely eliminating the custom-silicon threat.

articles.title: TSS Inc. (TSSI) Is Quietly Rewiring Its Business Around AI Data Centers
articles.summary: On August 13, TSS Inc. (NASDAQ:TSSI) reported second-quarter results that look worse on the top line and better underneath it. Revenue fell 20% year over yea...
articles.body:
On August 13, TSS Inc. (NASDAQ: TSSI ) reported second-quarter results that look worse on the top line and better underneath it. Revenue fell 20% year over year to $35.1 million, yet gross profit rose 11% and adjusted EBITDA climbed 12%. The company is deliberately walking away from lower-margin procurement work and leaning into systems integration for AI and HPC infrastructure, a business that grew 46% in the quarter. That trade-off is the whole story right now, and it cuts both ways.

Systems integration revenue reached $13.9 million in the quarter, up 46% from a year earlier, and now makes up 39% of revenue, versus just 22% in last year's second quarter. Facilities management grew even faster, up 84% to $2.7 million. CEO Darryll Dewan said systems integration is expected to keep outpacing the rest of the business given strong demand and the company's track record on complex technology projects.

TSS has started deploying capital toward a planned $17 million investment aimed at the next wave of AI data center technology, a buildout the company expects to start converting into higher systems integration revenue in the third quarter. The company has also put an idle asset back to work: its former Round Rock integration facility began warehouse operations on May 1, generating $0.3 million in operating lease income during the quarter.

Management is also pointing to stronger months ahead. TSS expects the second half of 2026 to outperform the first half, with accelerated systems integration growth, and it maintained guidance for full-year adjusted EBITDA to land between $20 million and $22 million, at the high end of that band.

The revenue decline is not small. Procurement revenue, still TSS's largest segment by dollars, fell 45% to $18.2 million in the quarter and is down 53% to $58.2 million for the first six months of the year. That drop pulled total revenue down 20% in the quarter and 37% for the year to date, to $90.5 million, even as the higher-margin segments expanded.

Profitability also slipped on a per-share basis. Second quarter net income was $1.4 million, or $0.05 per diluted share, compared with $1.5 million and $0.06 per diluted share a year earlier, after the company began recording a full tax provision following the removal of a deferred tax asset valuation allowance in the fourth quarter of 2025. For the first six months of 2026, net income fell to $3.7 million and diluted EPS to $0.13, down from $4.5 million and $0.17 in the prior year period.

articles.title: Nvidia's cash could reshape an AI cloud contender
articles.summary: A reported funding round would deepen ties between the chipmaker and a fast-growing compute supplier.
articles.body:
Startups spend years courting brand-name investors to build credibility before they go public. Rarely does one of those investors also happen to be the company's biggest supplier, and in a roundabout way, one of its own paying customers.

Nscale, a two-year-old British AI cloud computing firm, is negotiating to raise up to $3.5 billion ahead of a planned U.S. stock listing, according to Bloomberg .

Nvidia (NVDA) is expected to supply about $2 billion of that financing, with hedge fund Third Point leading a separate tranche of convertible notes and Goldman Sachs running the process .

The arrangement would make Nscale's chip supplier one of its largest shareholders just weeks before the company asks public investors to back a valuation roughly double its last private round.

Nvidia's money comes with a built-in customer

Nscale has ordered about 194,000 of Nvidia's upcoming Vera Rubin GPUs for its data centers.

Nvidia investing directly in the company placing that order blurs the line between a chip sale and an equity stake, since the revenue Nscale eventually books from renting out those chips flows partly from cash Nvidia supplied in the first place.

This isn't a new playbook. Nvidia used a similar structure with CoreWeave before that company's 2025 IPO, taking an equity stake and placing a $250 million anchor order inside the listing itself, according to CNBC .

Critics labeled that arrangement circular financing at the time, and 24/7WallSt reported Nvidia has since applied the same approach to other infrastructure buyers including Nokia and Nebius.

Microsoft and Google already said no to this deal

Nscale's biggest contract, a six-year, $45 billion deal to supply computing capacity to Anthropic, followed two earlier offers to bigger customers, according to Semafor .

Microsoft and Google were both in talks for that same capacity at Nscale's West Virginia campus before Anthropic took it, Semafor reported.

Microsoft walked away during a review of its data center portfolio, and Google passed after reassessing its own spending plans, according to the same report.

That history matters more than the headline number. A contract that two of the world's best-capitalized cloud companies considered and turned down is now the centerpiece of the pitch Nscale is making to public market investors, who have far less insight into Nscale's operations than Microsoft and Google had when they walked away.

articles.title: Autonomous excavators are digging with empty cabs
articles.summary: Bedrock Robotics says its autonomous excavators are doing paid earthwork on active job sites in Texas and Nevada with no operator in the cab.
articles.body: If you have ever driven past a construction site and watched an excavator moving huge piles of dirt, you probably figured there was an experienced operator sitting in the cab. On some job sites in Texas and Nevada, there is nobody in that seat. San Francisco-based Bedrock Robotics has autonomous excavators doing real commercial earthwork with no operator onboard. The company says the deployments follow a year of testing on active job sites with human supervision. Seeing AI take over software tasks is one thing. Watching it control a massive excavator on a live construction site feels very different. Bedrock says this could help contractors deal with worker shortages and keep projects moving more efficiently. Here's how the technology works and what could come next. Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats , has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed. Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com 100 KODIAK DRIVERLESS TRUCKS ARE HEADED FOR PUBLIC ROADS Bedrock's autonomous excavators are working on real projects Bedrock says its operator-free excavators are now active on major infrastructure projects. One machine is working on a Nevada water treatment facility with Sundt Construction. In Texas, Bedrock is working with Champion Site Prep on a multimillion-cubic-yard earthwork project. The company also has a 1.2 million-cubic-yard civil sitework project with Zachry Construction Corporation. The current work centers on rough early earthmoving and foundation prep. The company is concentrating on clearing earth, cut-and-fill operations and rough cuts before moving into more detailed work. That makes sense because earthwork comes early in a project. If crews fall behind there, everything that follows can feel the delay. Bedrock says productivity is approaching human levels Bedrock measures excavator productivity by the cubic yards of earth moved during a shift, a company spokesperson tells CyberGuy. How much earth a machine should move depends on the project, soil conditions and the rest of the equipment involved. Still, the spokesperson says, "As of our deployments in August 2026, two years after the company was founded, we are already near human-level productivity." How the Bedrock Operator makes an excavator autonomous Bedrock calls its system the Bedrock Operator. The company designed it as a retrofit for existing heavy equipment. Bedrock says crews can install its sensor and computing package in a day without permanent changes to the machine. Once a site manager sets the initial plan, the software takes over the digging work. Bedrock says its machine-learning system can understand the surrounding area and plan movement. It can then carry out complex tasks. The company says it trained the system on tens of thousands of hours of field work. However, there is an important detail about the current rollout. Bedrock is deploying new excavators that it outfitted and tested at its own facilities. When we asked when the system would begin operating on contractors' existing equipment, a Bedrock spokesperson said the company has no update to share yet but hopes to have more soon. So the retrofit model remains central to Bedrock's plan. The live operator-free deployments are still in an earlier phase. An empty cab still comes with human oversight Seeing a huge excavator move with nobody inside will probably make some people nervous. Bedrock knows safety will help determine how far this technology goes and says it comes first as the company expands deployment. The machines monitor their own progress while they work. If a machine gets stuck or cannot continue, the system can call for help. When we asked how often a person needs to step in, a Bedrock spokesperson told CyberGuy, "It's relatively rare." If a machine encounters something unusual or gets stuck, someone monitoring the fleet can briefly intervene until the autonomous system is ready to take back over. Bedrock also keeps a person in the loop. That gives the system a path to human support without requiring someone to sit in the cab all day. On active sites, that becomes especially important. People walk through work zones. Water trucks and other heavy equipment move nearby. Bedrock says the safety response happens automatically. "If a person or unauthorized object gets too close to a Bedrock-equipped machine, the machine will automatically stop," the spokesperson said. The excavator stays stopped until the person or object has moved to a safe distance, with no manual intervention required. HUMANLESS BIG RIG COMPLETES FIRST US FREIGHT RUN Why Bedrock started with one of the hardest machines Bedrock picked excavators for a reason. The company says excavators can account for about 25% of a contractor's fleet. They also take years to master. Bedrock estimates that an operator may need five years or more to fully develop the skill. That creates a difficult staffing problem. Contractors need experienced people, yet many projects involve long stretches of repetitive earthmoving. Bedrock wants autonomous equipment to handle more of that repeatable production work. Skilled operators could then focus on detailed jobs or supervise a larger operation. We have seen autonomous excavators before. CyberGuy previously covered HEAP, a 12-ton robotic excavator that built a massive stone wall on its own. What makes Bedrock different is where the technology is headed now. These excavators are doing commercial work on active job sites as part of real infrastructure projects. Construction faces a growing worker shortage The timing helps explain why investors are pouring money into this technology. Bedrock has raised more than $350 million. Its founding team includes former Waymo engineers who spent years working on autonomous vehicles. Meanwhile, construction companies are struggling to find enough skilled workers. Bedrock cites industry estimates showing that roughly one in five construction workers is over age 55. Another estimate says more than 40% of the construction workforce could retire within the next five years. The company also points to research showing that 92% of firms with open craft positions have difficulty filling at least some of those jobs. Those departures could hit contractors while demand remains high across many types of building projects. Costs add another pressure point. Bedrock cites a McKinsey analysis that found large construction projects typically took 20% longer than scheduled and ran up to 80% over budget. Then there is safety. Construction accounts for a disproportionate share of workplace deaths compared with its share of the overall workforce. Automation could help reduce exposure to dangerous tasks. However, companies will still need to prove that autonomous machines can work safely around people over long periods. Bedrock also takes a firm position on what this technology means for equipment operators. "We do not expect operators to be replaced at all," a Bedrock spokesperson tells CyberGuy. In the near term, the company sees Bedrock-equipped machines working alongside existing crews because contractors do not have enough skilled operators to tackle every project. Longer term, Bedrock expects some experienced operators to move into supervisory positions overseeing autonomous equipment. The company compares that future role to becoming a "foreman for machines." At the same time, Bedrock says people who want to continue operating equipment themselves should still have a place in construction for years to come. Bedrock wants machines to work together next The long-term idea goes far beyond one excavator digging by itself. Bedrock wants multiple machines to coordinate across a job site. Bedrock co-founder Kevin Peterson described a future where an excavator could work alongside a bulldozer, truck and grader. Instead of each machine operating as a separate tool, software could help coordinate the larger job. That could change project scheduling in a big way. A site manager might eventually assign the goal while a connected fleet determines how to move the work forward. Bedrock says this coordinated model remains on its roadmap. For now, the company is scaling excavator deployments and expanding the types of tasks its system can perform. What this means to you Here's why this could affect you. Construction delays can hold up new housing, road projects and water infrastructure. If autonomous equipment can keep earthwork moving when contractors cannot find enough experienced operators, some projects could move faster and stay closer to schedule. Bedrock says it sees autonomous machines working alongside people rather than eliminating operator jobs. In the near term, that could give existing crews more help with repetitive earthwork. Over time, some experienced operators could end up supervising groups of autonomous machines while others continue working directly in the cab. Permits and material shortages can still slow a project down. Skilled workers also remain essential for planning, detailed work and handling situations the technology cannot manage on its own. I'll be watching whether that near-human productivity holds up as these machines move onto more job sites. Bedrock says human intervention is relatively rare today, but I also want to see how that changes when one person is monitoring a larger fleet. Safety will be the other big test. I want to see what happens when something unexpected enters the work zone. The more autonomous equipment we put around people, the more important that real-world track record becomes. Kurt's key takeaways What catches my attention here is that Bedrock has moved beyond showing what an autonomous excavator might be able to do someday. These machines are already doing paid work on active construction sites with nobody sitting in the cab. Bedrock now tells us the machines are nearing human-level productivity and that human intervention is "relatively rare." Those are encouraging signs, but I want to see how those claims hold up across more projects and over longer periods. I also like hearing Bedrock say directly that it does not expect operators to disappear. If autonomy helps contractors handle more work while experienced people take on tougher jobs or supervise the machines, there could be a real upside for both crews and the projects they build. The real test will come as Bedrock puts more of these machines to work. If they stay safe and productive around real crews, those empty cabs may become a much more familiar sight. articles.title: NVIDIA (NVDA)’s $20 Billion Groq Bet Goes Live This Year With New AI Racks

articles.body:
CNBC reported that NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA )'s Groq 3 LPX rack is in full production and will be deployed alongside its Vera CPUs and Rubin GPUs at neocloud Nebius later this year, Nvidia senior director Dion Harris told reporters.

The rack marks the commercialization of technology from Nvidia's $20 billion purchase of Groq's assets in December, its largest deal on record. Each liquid-cooled rack packages 256 Groq chips. Nvidia said the rack can deliver 3,400 tokens per second, noting a benchmark from Artificial Analysis. Groq's chips are manufactured by Samsung, unlike Nvidia's own GPUs, which are made by Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co.

The $20 billion Groq deal represents a manageable financial risk for NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) relative to the strategic capabilities it could add to the company. Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon told CNBC that Nvidia is financially strong enough to absorb a deal of this size with little impact on its overall position. That gives Nvidia the flexibility to make large strategic investments while expanding into new AI chip technologies without materially straining its balance sheet.

Groq's technology extends Nvidia's dominance across the full AI compute stack rather than creating a rival product line. LPX handles low-latency inference while Nvidia's GPUs continue handling training and large-context processing. The rack can pair with Vera Rubin chips without customers changing their CUDA workflows, deepening the software lock-in that has made Nvidia hard to displace.

Execution has been fast, which matters in a market moving this quickly. Nvidia went from announcing the Groq purchase in December to full production and a named customer, Nebius, in eight months. It is a pace that shows Nvidia can absorb acquired technology and ship it rather than let it stall in integration.

Nvidia's inference speed now has a quantified edge over a key rival's approach. The Groq rack's 3,400 tokens per second compares with the 750 tokens per second OpenAI has promised for its Cerebras-powered "Ultrafast" mode. It gives Nvidia a benchmark it can point to as cloud providers shop for faster, more responsive AI inference.

NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) paid $20 billion for Groq's technology and talent without acquiring the company itself. Since Nvidia licensed Groq's technology and hired its employees rather than purchasing Groq outright, investors have less visibility into the full value of what Nvidia obtained and whether the transaction can generate returns proportionate to its unusually large price tag.

articles.title: Adobe ends an 18-year era as AI pressure mounts
articles.summary: Adobe makes major change after years of stock pain
articles.body:
Adobe is handing over control to a new CEO after the current CEO spent 18 years in the role, as artificial intelligence is set to disrupt the software company that powers Photoshop and Creative Cloud.

Adobe (ADBE) is undergoing one of its largest leadership overhauls ever at a particularly challenging time for investors.

Anil Chakravarthy will become president and CEO of software giant Adobe, succeeding Shantanu Narayen, who has been at the helm for more than 18 years. Chakravarthy will take over on Dec. 1, and Narayen will move to the role of executive chair.

But Wall Street's response hinted at the scale of the task confronting Adobe's new boss.

Adobe shares fell nearly 7% on Sept. 4, after the leadership announcement and David Wadhwani's departure. Wadhwani ran Adobe's creativity and productivity business and was a potential CEO candidate.

After falling more than 21% in 2025, the stock had fallen 18% in 2026 before Friday Sept 4.

But the greater issue is that generative AI is coming for the industry that Adobe has controlled for decades, and investors are waiting for proof that Adobe can transform its own AI technologies into enough growth to secure its business.

Adobe's leadership shakeup comes at a critical moment

Chakravarthy joined Adobe in 2020 after serving as CEO of Informatica. He oversaw Adobe's Digital Experience business first, then ran international field operations and finally led its Customer Experience Orchestration business.

That background might be a key hint as to where Adobe is headed.

Adobe says it's using agentic AI more in its corporate solutions to tailor interactions enterprises have with their consumers.

Narayen described Chakravarthy as a "transformational leader" with profound knowledge of Adobe's business.

But the succession also heralds another big shift.

Wadhwani, who has overseen Adobe's creative and productivity division for almost five years, said he was stepping down after Chakravarthy's appointment. Wadhwani was said to be a possible contender for the CEO role.

So Adobe is not just replacing the CEO. The corporation is also facing what may be the largest technical challenge to its creative-software brand since cloud computing emerged.

Now investors have to decide whether Chakravarthy can take that disruption and reshape it once again.

Wall Street sees a major AI threat to Adobe

Adobe's main challenge is that it lacks artificial intelligence.

The business has been working hard to grow Firefly and add generative AI capabilities to products like Photoshop and its larger creative suite.

articles.title: When AI Saves Time At Work, Who Gets To Keep It?
articles.summary: AI is changing who captures productivity gains at work. As AI saves time and expands individual capability, freelancing may challenge the traditional employm...
articles.body:
If AI lets you finish a full day's work before lunch, who owns the afternoon?

Most companies already have an answer. The workday stays eight hours no matter how quickly the work gets done. Extra capacity becomes room for more tasks, not free time. But alongside organizations, the independent economy is generating a new answer. For an independent consultant who agrees to deliver a project for a set fee, when AI cuts the job from eight hours to four, those four hours belong to them. They can take another client, learn something new, spend the afternoon with their kids, or simply stop working for the day.

AI is starting to sever the link between the time a job takes and the value it produces, and that link sits at the heart of the traditional employment relationship.

How AI Is Changing Who Benefits From Productivity Gains

Every significant productivity improvement creates a dividend — something that once required more time, people or resources can now be produced with less. Employers have traditionally been in the strongest position to decide how that dividend is used: faster tools increase throughput, better systems allow the same workforce to produce more, productivity gains become part of the economics of the organization. That made sense when the productive infrastructure largely belonged to the company, when the machines, software, information, systems, distribution and support structures that made people more productive were organizational assets.

AI changes that relationship because a growing share of productive capability is now in the hands of the individual. A marketer can use AI to research, analyze, draft and test work that once required several specialists. A developer can move through more of the build cycle independently. A consultant can produce work that once justified hiring a firm. None of that capability stays locked inside company walls. The same person can use it on their own time, for their own clients, building their own income, and decide for themselves whether to fill the hours AI frees up or simply not work them at all.

The difference between employment and independent work has always existed. AI is widening that gap in ways that are becoming impossible to ignore.

How AI Is Making Freelancing A Stronger Alternative To Employment

An Anthropic survey of more than 80,000 Claude users found that when people reported who benefited from their AI-driven productivity, they usually meant themselves, not their employer. Only about one in ten said the gain mainly went to an employer or client. Inside a traditional employment contract, though, the organization is generally in the strongest position to decide what happens to those gains. Which is probably why we're seeing 66% of employees stay online to hide the time AI saves them because they know visible gains become additional workload. Anthropic's data also show that the people feeling the biggest gains were also more likely to worry about their own job security. That combination — feeling more capable and less secure at the same time — is exactly what pushes someone to ask what their skills are worth outside the building they currently work in.

articles.title: Apple (AAPL)’s New Mac Mini and Studio Bet Big on On-Device AI
articles.summary: CNBC reported that Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL) announced new Mac Mini and Mac Studio models with updated chips built for AI workloads. The Mac Mini now offers A...
articles.body:
CNBC reported that Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL ) announced new Mac Mini and Mac Studio models with updated chips built for AI workloads.

The Mac Mini now offers Apple's new M6 chip, its first built on a 2-nanometer process, or an M5 Pro, and starts at $899, up from $799 for the prior model. Apple says the M6 delivers 4 times faster AI performance and 2 times faster graphics than the M4 model it replaces, while the M5 Pro can process large language model prompts up to 8.5 times faster than the M2 Pro version. The Mac Studio now starts at $2,499 with the M5 Max chip or $5,499 with the new M5 Ultra, up from $5,299 for the prior Ultra model, and multiple M5 Ultra units can be linked together to pool memory for running large AI models. "With these frameworks and new chips, developers can run and fine-tune large AI models locally on their Mac," Apple said. Preorders opened Tuesday, with units shipping September 22.

The performance gains here are substantial, not incremental. The M6 chip delivers 4 times faster AI performance and is Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s first chip built on a 2-nanometer process. The M5 Pro configuration processes large language model prompts 8.5 times faster than the model it replaces, Apple's own specifications show, giving Apple genuine technical claims to back its AI-focused marketing.

Apple is showing pricing power even as component costs rise industry-wide. Despite memory and silicon shortages pushing costs higher across the industry, Apple raised prices on both product lines rather than absorbing the cost pressure itself. It is a sign the company believes demand can bear higher price points.

These desktops are becoming more strategically important to Apple than their revenue alone suggests. It shows how Mac desktops have become a foothold in the AI development world for Apple. It is a showcase for its custom silicon that can influence which platform developers build AI tools on and an ecosystem benefit that extends beyond the sale of any individual machine.

The price increases land directly on the customer, not on Apple Inc. (NASDAQ: AAPL )'s margin cushion since the Mac Mini's entry price has risen from $599 at its 2024 launch to $899 now, a jump of roughly 50% in two years. The increases are linked to memory and silicon cost pressures rather than a deliberate premium repositioning. It means Apple may be passing through cost increases rather than capturing additional margin.

Mac desktops remain a small part of Apple's overall business regardless of how compelling the AI upgrades are. Mac Mini and Mac Studio sales are a fraction of what iPhone contributes to Apple's revenue, so even meaningful technical improvements to these product lines are unlikely to move Apple's overall financial results in any given quarter.

articles.title: Musk Moves Up SpaceX (SPCX)’s Orbital Data Center Timeline, Again
articles.summary: Bloomberg reported that Elon Musk said Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ:SPCX) first AI satellites, powered exclusively by NVIDIA Corporation (NAS...
articles.body:
Bloomberg reported that Elon Musk said Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX ) first AI satellites, powered exclusively by NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ: NVDA ) chips, will launch in the fourth quarter of 2027 and reach "significant scale" in 2028, citing a post on X. Musk wrote "SpaceX, in partnership with Nvidia, has designed a space-optimized Vera Rubin NVL72 system for launch to orbit in Q4 next year," describing the satellite data center as "significantly simpler, lower cost, denser, and lighter than a traditional rack."

The timeline has moved up twice since SpaceX's May IPO prospectus, which targeted "as early as 2028," and Musk's August 4 earnings call comments, which said launches would begin "next year." SpaceX COO Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC ahead of the IPO that the firm has already struck deals with Anthropic and Google to rent out orbital compute capacity.

The timeline is moving earlier, not later, which is unusual for a space infrastructure project. Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX ) pulled its target forward from as early as 2028 in its IPO prospectus to a specific Q4 2027 date within a few months. The acceleration shows SpaceX believes development is progressing faster than previously expected and could bring orbital computing revenue online sooner than investors initially anticipated.

Real customers have already committed before SpaceX launches a single satellite. SpaceX President Gwynne Shotwell told CNBC that the company has struck deals with Anthropic and Google to rent orbital compute capacity. It shows that major AI companies already see potential value in the technology. Those early commitments could reduce demand risk if SpaceX delivers the planned capacity.

Wall Street sees a large long-term opportunity if the technology works as described. JPMorgan analyst Doug Anmuth projected SpaceX could pursue roughly 75 gigawatts of orbital compute by the end of 2031 at a significantly cheaper cost than could be done on Earth a scale that would make this a meaningful new revenue stream beyond SpaceX's existing launch and Starlink businesses.

Musk has a well-documented history of missing his own aggressive timelines. The Tesla Roadster, first shown in 2017, still has not shipped, and both the Cybertruck and Tesla Semi arrived years behind their original target dates, a track record that argues for treating any specific quarter Musk names as directional rather than firm.

The basic economics remain undisclosed and unproven, and Musk has said the orbital rack will cost less than traditional ground-based infrastructure. But Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ: SPCX ) has not disclosed enough detail to show whether those savings will outweigh the costs of launching, powering, cooling, maintaining, and replacing orbital computing hardware. Without demonstrated unit economics, investors cannot determine whether orbital data centers will become a highly profitable business or an expensive technological experiment.

articles.title: Authors push back as publishers and agents make claims on Anthropic settlement | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Authors say publishers seem to be claiming more than their fair share of settlement payments.
articles.body:
Some authors hoping to receive their share of Anthropic’s $1.5 billion copyright settlement said they received surprising emails this week — emails informing them that someone else was making a claim on their payments.

Anthropic settled a copyright class action suit last year, after a judge ruled that training AI models on copyrighted material is legal under fair use doctrine, but pirating that material was not. The deal received final approval in July, allowing the payments to move forward.

Under the terms of the settlement, the authors of nearly 500,000 titles will be paid $3,000 for each pirated work. If the book is still in-print with a traditional publisher, the money will be split 50-50 between author and publisher. If the book was self-published, or if the publisher reverted the rights by allowing the book to go out-of-print, then the author should get the entire payment.

But writers have been posting on social media that publishers seem to be claiming more than their fair share of some payments. For example, mystery and thriller author April Henry asked , “WTF is HarperCollins playing at? They claimed one of my books on the Anthropic Settlement that reverted back at least 17 years ago AND on the same day I got a credit alert saying they had been added as my employer! (which they never were).”

At the popular blog Writers Beware , Victoria Strauss wrote that she’s been receiving author complaints that fall into two broad categories: one where publishers are seeking payment for works that they no longer have a legitimate claim on (because the rights have reverted), and another where publishers are seeking a full 100% payment when they’re only entitled to 50%.

In both cases, Strauss said she’s “reluctant to attribute to malice what can be plausibly explained by poor recordkeeping” — and she noted that some publishers have already said this is a mistake that they’ve asked Anthropic to fix.

Similarly, Authors Guild CEO Mary Rasenberger told The New York Times that she doesn’t see this as “a grab by the publishers” and that she doesn’t believe publishers are “specifically trying to screw any author over.” Instead, she argued that this is the predictable result of bad record-keeping and a confusing settlement process.

Strauss also acknowledged that any complaints she’s seen are just “a peek through a small crack in a massive wall.”

“But the unusually large number of reports I’ve received over the last two days, as well as the fact that authors are reporting the exact same errors over and over, suggest to me that these aren’t the kind of routine glitches you might expect from such a large operation, but something much more wide[s]pread and systemic,” she wrote.

And publishers aren’t the only ones seeking a cut of the payments. Strauss said she’s gotten complaints that a number of literary agencies are also making claims, which she said is surprising since “agents are not rightsholders in the books that they sell.”

Author Courtney Milan (the pen name of former law clerk and law professor Heidi Bond) was more blunt in a post on Bluesky , writing, “Apparently some agents are trying to claim percentages on the Anthropic settlement, and I do not REMOTELY think they should do this, what the fuck, stop that shit!”

Milan and the Authors Guild also shared more details about how authors can dispute their payment allocations. (One tricky issue: When the rights to a specific book reverted. In order for an author to make a 100% claim on a book, the rights reversion needs to have happened before August 10, 2022, which is the “download date” in the settlement.)
